chapters.title: Arjuna Visada Yoga
chapters.fullSummary:
The first chapter of the Bhagavad Gita - "Arjuna Vishada Yoga" introduces the setup, the setting, the characters and the circumstances that led to the epic battle of Mahabharata, fought between the Pandavas and the Kauravas. It outlines the reasons that led to the revelation of the of Bhagavad Gita.
As both armies stand ready for the battle, the mighty warrior Arjuna, on observing the warriors on both sides becomes increasingly sad and depressed due to the fear of losing his relatives and friends and the consequent sins attributed to killing his own relatives. So, he surrenders to Lord Krishna, seeking a solution. Thus, follows the wisdom of the Bhagavad Gita.

chapters.title: Sankhya Yoga
chapters.fullSummary:
The second chapter of the Bhagavad Gita is "Sankhya Yoga". This is the most important chapter of the Bhagavad Gita as Lord Krishna condenses the teachings of the entire Gita in this chapter. This chapter is the essence of the entire Gita. 
"Sankhya Yoga" can be categorized into 4 main topics - 
1. Arjuna completely surrenders himself to Lord Krishna and accepts his position as a disciple and Krishna as his Guru. He requests Krishna to guide him on how to dismiss his sorrow.
2. Explanation of the main cause of all grief, which is ignorance of the true nature of Self.
3. Karma Yoga - the discipline of selfless action without being attached to its fruits.
4. Description of a Perfect Man - One whose mind is steady and one-pointed.

chapters.title: Karma Yoga
chapters.fullSummary: The third chapter of the Bhagavad Gita is "Karma Yoga" or the "Path of Selfless Service". Here Lord Krishna emphasizes the importance of karma in life. He reveals that it is important for every human being to engage in some sort of activity in this material world. Further, he describes the kinds of actions that lead to bondage and the kinds that lead to liberation. Those persons who continue to perform their respective duties externally for the pleasure of the Supreme, without attachment to its rewards get liberation at the end.

chapters.title: Jnana Karma Sanyasa Yoga
chapters.summary: Path of Knowledge and the Disciplines of Action
chapters.fullSummary: The fourth chapter of the Bhagavad Gita is "Jnana Karma Sanyasa Yoga". In this chapter, Krishna glorifies the Karma Yoga and imparts the Transcendental Knowledge (the knowledge of the soul and the Ultimate Truth) to Arjuna. He reveals the reason behind his appearance in this material world. He reveals that even though he is eternal, he reincarnates time after time to re-establish dharma and peace on this Earth. His births and activities are eternal and are never contaminated by material flaws. Those persons who know and understand this Truth engage in his devotion with full faith and eventually attain Him. They do not have to take birth in this world again.

chapters.title: Karma Sanyasa Yoga
chapters.fullSummary: The fifth chapter of the Bhagavad Gita is "Karma Sanyasa Yoga". In this chapter, Krishna compares the paths of renunciation in actions (Karma Sanyas) and actions with detachment (Karma Yoga) and explains that both are means to reach the same goal and we can choose either. A wise person should perform his/her worldly duties without attachment to the fruits of his/her actions and dedicate them to God. This way they remain unaffected by sin and eventually attain liberation.

chapters.title: Dhyana Yoga
chapters.fullSummary: The sixth chapter of the Bhagavad Gita is "Dhyana Yoga". In this chapter, Krishna reveals the "Yoga of Meditation" and how to practise this Yoga. He discusses the role of action in preparing for Meditation, how performing duties in devotion purifies one's mind and heightens one's spiritual consciousness. He explains in detail the obstacles that one faces when trying to control their mind and the exact methods by which one can conquer their mind. He reveals how one can focus their mind on Paramatma and unite with the God.

chapters.title: Gyaan Vigyana Yoga
chapters.fullSummary: The seventh chapter of the Bhagavad Gita is "Gyaan Vigyana Yoga ". In this chapter, Krishna reveals that he is the Supreme Truth, the principal cause and the sustaining force of everything. He reveals his illusionary energy in this material world called Maya, which is very difficult to overcome but those who surrender their minds unto Him attain Him easily. He also describes the four types of people who surrender to Him in devotion and the four kinds that don't. Krishna confirms that He is the Ultimate Reality and those who realize this Truth reach the pinnacle of spiritual realization and unite with the Lord.

chapters.title: Akshara Brahma Yoga
chapters.fullSummary: The eighth chapter of the Bhagavad Gita is "Akshara Brahma Yoga". In this chapter, Krishna reveals the importance of the last thought before death. If we can remember Krishna at the time of death, we will certainly attain him. Thus, it is very important to be in constant awareness of the Lord at all times, thinking of Him and chanting His names at all times. By perfectly absorbing their mind in Him through constant devotion, one can go beyond this material existence to Lord's Supreme abode.

chapters.title: Raja Vidya Yoga
chapters.summary: Yoga through the King of Sciences
chapters.fullSummary: The ninth chapter of the Bhagavad Gita is "Raja Vidya Yoga". In this chapter, Krishna explains that He is Supreme and how this material existence is created, maintained and destroyed by His Yogmaya and all beings come and go under his supervision. He reveals the Role and the Importance of Bhakti (transcendental devotional service) towards our Spiritual Awakening. In such devotion, one must live for the God, offer everything that he possesses to Him and do everything for Him only. One who follows such devotion becomes free from the bonds of this material world and unites with the Lord.

chapters.title: Vibhooti Yoga
chapters.summary: Yoga through Appreciating the Infinite Opulences of God
chapters.fullSummary: The tenth chapter of the Bhagavad Gita is "Vibhooti Yoga". In this chapter, Krishna reveals Himself as the cause of all causes. He describes His various manifestations and opulences in order to increase Arjuna's Bhakti. Arjuna is fully convinced of Lord's paramount position and proclaims him to be the Supreme Personality. He prays to Krishna to describe more of His divine glories which are like nectar to hear.

chapters.title: Vishwaroopa Darshana Yoga
chapters.summary: Yoga through Beholding the Cosmic Form of God
chapters.fullSummary: The eleventh chapter of the Bhagavad Gita is "Vishwaroopa Darshana Yoga". In this chapter, Arjuna requests Krishna to reveal His Universal Cosmic Form that encompasses all the universes, the entire existence. Arjuna is granted divine vision to be able to see the entirety of creation in the body of the Supreme Lord Krishna.

chapters.title: Bhakti Yoga
chapters.fullSummary: The twelfth chapter of the Bhagavad Gita is "Bhakti Yoga". In this chapter, Krishna emphasizes the superiority of Bhakti Yoga (the path of devotion) over all other types of spiritual disciplines and reveals various aspects of devotion. He further explains that the devotees who perform pure devotional service to Him, with their consciousness, merged in Him and all their actions dedicated to Him, are quickly liberated from the cycle of life and death. He also describes the various qualities of the devotees who are very dear to Him.

chapters.title: Ksetra Ksetrajna Vibhaaga Yoga
chapters.summary: Yoga through Distinguishing the Field and the Knower of the Field
chapters.fullSummary: The thirteenth chapter of the Bhagavad Gita is "Ksetra Ksetrajna Vibhaaga Yoga". The word "kshetra" means "the field", and the "kshetrajna" means "the knower of the field". We can think of our material body as the field and our immortal soul as the knower of the field. In this chapter, Krishna discriminates between the physical body and the immortal soul. He explains that the physical body is temporary and perishable whereas the soul is permanent and eternal. The physical body can be destroyed but the soul can never be destroyed. The chapter then describes God, who is the Supreme Soul. All the individual souls have originated from the Supreme Soul. One who clearly understands the difference between the body, the Soul and the Supreme Soul attains the realization of Brahman.

chapters.title: Gunatraya Vibhaga Yoga
chapters.summary: Yoga through Understanding the Three Modes of Material Nature
chapters.fullSummary: The fourteenth chapter of the Bhagavad Gita is "Gunatraya Vibhaga Yoga". In this chapter, Krishna reveals the three gunas (modes) of the material nature - goodness, passion and ignorance which everything in the material existence is influenced by. He further explains the essential characteristics of each of these modes, their cause and how they influence a living entity affected by them. He then reveals the various characteristics of the persons who have gone beyond these gunas. The chapter ends with Krishna reminding us of the power of pure devotion to God and how attachment to God can help us transcend these gunas.

chapters.title: Purushottama Yoga
chapters.summary: The Yoga of the Supreme Divine Personality
chapters.fullSummary: The fifteenth chapter of the Bhagavad Gita is "Purushottama Yoga". In Sanskrit, Purusha means the "All-pervading God", and Purushottam means the timeless & transcendental aspect of God.        Krishna reveals that the purpose of this Transcendental knowledge of the God is to detach ourselves from the bondage of the material world and to understand Krishna as the Supreme Divine Personality, who is the eternal controller and sustainer of the world. One who understands this Ultimate Truth surrenders to Him and engages in His devotional service.

chapters.title: Daivasura Sampad Vibhaga Yoga
chapters.summary: Yoga through Discerning the Divine and Demoniac Natures
chapters.fullSummary: The sixteenth chapter of the Bhagavad Gita is "Daivasura Sampad Vibhaga Yoga". In this chapter, Krishna describes explicitly the two kinds of natures among human beings - divine and demoniac. Those who possess demonaic qualities associate themselves with the modes of passion and ignorance do not follow the regulations of the scriptures and embrace materialistic views. These people attain lower births and further material bondage. But people who possess divine qualities, follow the instructions of the scriptures, associate themselves with the mode of goodness and purify the mind through spiritual practices. This leads to the enhancement of divine qualities and they eventually attain spiritual realization.

chapters.title: Sraddhatraya Vibhaga Yoga
chapters.summary: Yoga through Discerning the Three Divisions of Faith
chapters.fullSummary: The seventeenth chapter of the Bhagavad Gita is "Sraddhatraya Vibhaga Yoga". In this chapter, Krishna describes the three types of faith corresponding to the three modes of the material nature. Lord Krishna further reveals that it is the nature of faith that determines the quality of life and the character of living entities. Those who have faith in passion and ignorance perform actions that yield temporary, material results while those who have faith in goodness perform actions in accordance with scriptural instructions and hence their hearts get further purified.

chapters.title: Moksha Sanyaas Yoga
chapters.summary: Yoga through the Perfection of Renunciation and Surrender
chapters.fullSummary: The eighteenth chapter of the Bhagavad Gita is "Moksha Sanyas Yoga". Arjuna requests the Lord to explain the difference between the two types of renunciations - sanyaas(renunciation of actions) and tyaag(renunciation of desires). Krishna explains that a sanyaasi is one who abandons family and society in order to practise spiritual discipline whereas a tyaagi is one who performs their duties without attachment to the rewards of their actions and dedicating them to the God. Krishna recommends the second kind of renunciation - tyaag. Krishna then gives a detailed analysis of the effects of the three modes of material nature. He declares that the highest path of spirituality is pure, unconditional loving service unto the Supreme Divine Personality, Krishna. If we always remember Him, keep chanting His name and dedicate all our actions unto Him, take refuge in Him and make Him our Supreme goal, then by His grace, we will surely overcome all obstacles and difficulties and be freed from this cycle of birth and death.

1-1.sanskrit:
धृतराष्ट्र उवाच

धर्मक्षेत्रे कुरुक्षेत्रे समवेता युयुत्सवः।

मामकाः पाण्डवाश्चैव किमकुर्वत सञ्जय।।1.1।।
1-1.transliteration:
dhṛitarāśhtra uvācha
dharma-kṣhetre kuru-kṣhetre samavetā yuyutsavaḥ
māmakāḥ pāṇḍavāśhchaiva kimakurvata sañjaya

translation.simple: King Dhritarashtra asked Sanjaya, 'On the sacred field of Kurukshetra, where duty and truth were to be tested, my children and the Pandavas gathered, ready to fight. O Sanjaya, what transpired there?'
translation.deep: This opening verse quietly sets the stage for a journey of inner revelation. King Dhritarashtra, perhaps symbolizing the heart veiled by attachment, asks about the gathering on the sacred 'field of dharma.' Kurukshetra represents not just a historical ground, but the very arena of our own lives, where the spirit of duty and the pull of worldly desires meet. His gentle inquiry to Sanjaya reflects the soul's first stirrings of wonder, as it begins to witness the profound drama of existence unfold, guided by divine wisdom.
translation.essence: This verse gently begins the divine song, as a king, with a heart heavy with worldly ties, asks about the unfolding of destiny on the sacred field of dharma, inviting us to contemplate our own inner battles and the path of righteousness.

1-2.sanskrit:
सञ्जय उवाच

दृष्ट्वा तु पाण्डवानीकं व्यूढं दुर्योधनस्तदा।

आचार्यमुपसङ्गम्य राजा वचनमब्रवीत्।।1.2।।
1-2.transliteration:
sañjaya uvācha
dṛiṣhṭvā tu pāṇḍavānīkaṁ vyūḍhaṁ duryodhanastadā
āchāryamupasaṅgamya rājā vachanamabravīt

translation.simple: Sanjaya narrated: When King Duryodhana saw the Pandava forces arranged for battle, he approached his revered teacher, Dronacharya, and began to speak to him.
translation.deep: Sanjaya recounted the scene: King Duryodhana, beholding the Pandava army meticulously arrayed for conflict, turned to his respected teacher, Dronacharya. This initial approach, as he prepared to voice his heart's concerns, subtly marks the threshold where the external drama of war begins to merge with the timeless spiritual wisdom soon to be imparted.
translation.essence: The narrative unfolds: Seeing the opposing army, Duryodhana seeks his teacher, initiating the sacred dialogue of the Bhagavad Gita.

1-3.sanskrit:
पश्यैतां पाण्डुपुत्राणामाचार्य महतीं चमूम्।

व्यूढां द्रुपदपुत्रेण तव शिष्येण धीमता।।1.3।।
1-3.transliteration:
paśhyaitāṁ pāṇḍu-putrāṇām āchārya mahatīṁ chamūm
vyūḍhāṁ drupada-putreṇa tava śhiṣhyeṇa dhīmatā

translation.simple: Behold, dear teacher, the mighty assembly of the Pandavas. See how skillfully it has been arrayed by Drupada's son, your own perceptive student.
translation.deep: In this moment, where Duryodhana directs his guru's attention to the opposing army, we witness the complex tapestry of human relationships. He highlights the strength of the Pandavas, arrayed by a student Dronacharya himself guided. This reminds us that life's challenges often involve those we have known and cherished, inviting us to approach every situation with a heart open to understanding and a mind seeking inner peace, even amidst conflict.
translation.essence: A poignant scene unfolds as a leader asks his teacher to behold the formidable opposing forces, noting how the army is arrayed by the teacher's own gifted student. This moment gently guides us to reflect on the intricate bonds of karma and the quiet strength required to face life's inevitable tests with a tranquil spirit.

1-4.sanskrit:
अत्र शूरा महेष्वासा भीमार्जुनसमा युधि।

युयुधानो विराटश्च द्रुपदश्च महारथः।।1.4।।
1-4.transliteration:
atra śhūrā maheṣhvāsā bhīmārjuna-samā yudhi
yuyudhāno virāṭaśhcha drupadaśhcha mahā-rathaḥ

translation.simple: On this sacred battlefield, mighty archers stand, brave warriors as formidable as Bhima and Arjuna themselves. Among them are Yuyudhana, King Virata, and the great charioteer Drupada, all arrayed for the coming conflict.
translation.deep: Witnessing this array of powerful individuals, we are gently reminded that life too presents its own grand formations of challenges and strengths. Each 'warrior' we face, internal or external, serves as a prompt to deepen our faith and seek guidance from the ultimate source of all power.
translation.essence: Mighty warriors stand ready, reflecting the varied strengths in creation. May our hearts find peace knowing that beyond all earthly power, the Lord's grace eternally prevails.

1-5.sanskrit:
धृष्टकेतुश्चेकितानः काशिराजश्च वीर्यवान्।

पुरुजित्कुन्तिभोजश्च शैब्यश्च नरपुङ्गवः।।1.5।।
1-5.transliteration:
dhṛiṣhṭaketuśhchekitānaḥ kāśhirājaśhcha vīryavān
purujit kuntibhojaśhcha śhaibyaśhcha nara-puṅgavaḥ
yudhāmanyuśhcha vikrānta uttamaujāśhcha vīryavān

translation.simple: Among the noble warriors, we find Dhristaketu, Chekitana, and the valiant King of Kashi. Purujit, Kuntibhoja, and the respected Shaibya, a true leader among people, are also present.
translation.deep: In this sacred gathering, we observe the assembly of esteemed souls like Dhristaketu and Chekitana. The powerful King of Kashi, Purujit, Kuntibhoja, and Shaibya—a jewel among men—all stand ready. Their presence reminds us that diverse noble hearts align when a higher purpose calls for righteous action.
translation.essence: This verse quietly acknowledges the presence of many great warriors—Dhristaketu, Chekitana, the mighty King of Kashi, Purujit, Kuntibhoja, and the revered Shaibya—each a pillar of strength united for a divine cause.

1-6.sanskrit:
युधामन्युश्च विक्रान्त उत्तमौजाश्च वीर्यवान्।

सौभद्रो द्रौपदेयाश्च सर्व एव महारथाः।।1.6।।

translation.simple: Among them are the brave Yudhāmanyu and the mighty Uttamaujas. Also present are Abhimanyu, the dear son of Subhadrā, and the noble sons of Draupadī. Truly, each of these sacred souls is a great charioteer.
translation.deep: As we hear of these brave warriors—Yudhāmanyu, Uttamaujas, the beloved Abhimanyu, and Draupadī's sons—all described as great charioteers, we can reflect on the profound strength that gathers when truth is to be protected. Their presence on the field, each a master of their craft, speaks to the careful planning of the Divine, reminding us that all strength, skill, and courage ultimately serve a higher plan, even in moments of challenge.
translation.essence: This verse gently lists more of the valiant hearts on the side of righteousness, reassuring us that many strong and dedicated souls are always aligned with the path of dharma.

1-7.sanskrit:
अस्माकं तु विशिष्टा ये तान्निबोध द्विजोत्तम।

नायका मम सैन्यस्य संज्ञार्थं तान्ब्रवीमि ते।।1.7।।
1-7.transliteration:
asmākaṁ tu viśhiṣhṭā ye tānnibodha dwijottama
nāyakā mama sainyasya sanjñārthaṁ tānbravīmi te

translation.simple: O revered teacher, I wish to tell you about the most distinguished leaders among us. Please listen, for I shall name the commanders of my army for your information.
translation.deep: This verse, spoken by Duryodhana to his teacher, invites us to calmly observe and understand the distinct qualities and leadership present in any situation. It subtly prompts us to acknowledge all forces at play, discerning their nature with a peaceful heart as we navigate our spiritual journey.
translation.essence: It calls us to recognize and calmly comprehend the significant individuals or elements within our current circumstances, reflecting on the importance of clear awareness before action.

1-8.sanskrit:
भवान्भीष्मश्च कर्णश्च कृपश्च समितिञ्जयः।

अश्वत्थामा विकर्णश्च सौमदत्तिस्तथैव च।।1.8।।
1-8.transliteration:
bhavānbhīṣhmaśhcha karṇaśhcha kṛipaśhcha samitiñjayaḥ
aśhvatthāmā vikarṇaśhcha saumadattis tathaiva cha

translation.simple: Behold, O seeker, great souls are gathered: the revered Drona, the wise Bhishma, the valiant Karna, and Kripa, ever triumphant in battle. Also present are Ashwatthama, Vikarna, and Bhuriśravas.
translation.deep: This sacred verse names an impressive array of warriors, including revered teachers and powerful heroes. It quietly sets the stage for a momentous event, inviting us to contemplate how even the most cherished figures become part of life's grand challenges. It guides our reflection towards discerning true purpose amidst formidable strength, seeking wisdom beyond mere worldly power.
translation.essence: The gathering of these formidable figures reminds us that even in the face of great power and grand events, our spiritual journey calls us to inner peace and unwavering faith in the divine unfolding.

1-9.sanskrit:
अन्ये च बहवः शूरा मदर्थे त्यक्तजीविताः।

नानाशस्त्रप्रहरणाः सर्वे युद्धविशारदाः।।1.9।।
1-9.transliteration:
anye cha bahavaḥ śhūrā madarthe tyaktajīvitāḥ
nānā-śhastra-praharaṇāḥ sarve yuddha-viśhāradāḥ

translation.simple: Here also are many other brave warriors, ready to dedicate their lives. They are masters of various weapons, all truly skilled in the art of war.
translation.deep: Within these ranks stand numerous courageous souls, whose unwavering devotion prepares them to offer their very lives. Each one is a seasoned expert in the use of diverse weaponry, a true master of the battlefield. This scene reflects the depth of commitment and readiness for sacrifice that can inspire individuals, even as they face the profound challenges of their chosen path.
translation.essence: Many brave and highly skilled warriors, filled with profound dedication, stand ready for supreme sacrifice.

1-10.sanskrit:
अपर्याप्तं तदस्माकं बलं भीष्माभिरक्षितम्।

पर्याप्तं त्विदमेतेषां बलं भीमाभिरक्षितम्।।1.10।।
1-10.transliteration:
aparyāptaṁ tadasmākaṁ balaṁ bhīṣhmābhirakṣhitam
paryāptaṁ tvidameteṣhāṁ balaṁ bhīmābhirakṣhitam

translation.simple: Duryodhana felt his grand army, protected by the formidable Bhishma, was not quite enough. Yet, the Pandava's army, guarded by the mighty Bhima, seemed to him complete and sufficient.
translation.deep: This verse gently points to a subtle truth: true strength isn't always about visible numbers or the prowess of great warriors. Even a vast material force can be overshadowed by inner doubt and a sense of inadequacy if one's heart is not aligned with righteousness. Conversely, a smaller group, when blessed by dharma and divine presence, can possess an unshakeable inner sufficiency and calm.
translation.essence: Real strength flourishes not from external might, but from inner conviction, a righteous heart, and the grace of the Divine.

1-11.sanskrit:
अयनेषु च सर्वेषु यथाभागमवस्थिताः।

भीष्ममेवाभिरक्षन्तु भवन्तः सर्व एव हि।।1.11।।
1-11.transliteration:
ayaneṣhu cha sarveṣhu yathā-bhāgamavasthitāḥ
bhīṣhmamevābhirakṣhantu bhavantaḥ sarva eva hi

translation.simple: All of you, positioned in your designated places, must protect the revered Bhishma from all sides. This directive from the battlefield gently reminds us of our own duties. It encourages us to take our stand, fulfill our unique role with dedication, and safeguard what is dear and sacred in our lives.
translation.deep: Though spoken amidst preparations for war, this verse carries a deeper spiritual echo. It emphasizes the importance of unwavering focus and unity to protect what truly matters. Bhishma, the wise patriarch, can symbolize the divine wisdom or dharma we must collectively and individually guard within ourselves, ensuring its preservation against the internal and external battles of life. Each person's dedicated placement contributes to the whole, fostering a serene yet powerful defense of truth.
translation.essence: Stand steadfast in your divine duty, and with focused intent, safeguard the wisdom that illuminates your path.

1-12.sanskrit:
तस्य संजनयन्हर्षं कुरुवृद्धः पितामहः।

सिंहनादं विनद्योच्चैः शङ्खं दध्मौ प्रतापवान्।।1.12।।
1-12.transliteration:
tasya sañjanayan harṣhaṁ kuru-vṛiddhaḥ pitāmahaḥ
siṁha-nādaṁ vinadyochchaiḥ śhaṅkhaṁ dadhmau pratāpavān

translation.simple: As the great armies stood poised, the revered elder Bhishma, a mighty and wise presence, sounded his sacred conch shell. Its powerful call, like a lion's majestic roar, resonated across the field, filling Duryodhana's heart with a surge of joy and encouragement.
translation.deep: This powerful sound from Bhishma's conch is not just a battle cry; it represents a deep moment of commitment, the firm resolve with which a soul enters a significant phase of life. The resonant sound, heard across the vast field, invites us to reflect on our own inner calls to duty and purpose. It reminds us that even when facing immense challenges, one can act with unwavering strength and quiet determination, trusting in the unfolding of a greater plan.
translation.essence: The venerable Bhishma's majestic conch sound brought joy to Duryodhana, marking the solemn commencement of the righteous battle and the journey of destiny.

1-13.sanskrit:
ततः शङ्खाश्च भेर्यश्च पणवानकगोमुखाः।

सहसैवाभ्यहन्यन्त स शब्दस्तुमुलोऽभवत्।।1.13।।
1-13.transliteration:
tataḥ śhaṅkhāśhcha bheryaśhcha paṇavānaka-gomukhāḥ
sahasaivābhyahanyanta sa śhabdastumulo ’bhavat

translation.simple: Then, all at once, conch shells, various drums, and horn instruments were sounded. A vast and powerful sound arose, filling the air.
translation.deep: As these sacred instruments resounded, their collective sound was not merely a call to arms. It heralded a profound turning point, a moment when the divine play was about to unfold with great intensity. In this deep resonance, one could sense the very fabric of destiny being stirred.
translation.essence: This profound surge of sound announced the arrival of a momentous turning point, a powerful declaration that the divine narrative was now fully set in motion.

1-14.sanskrit:
ततः श्वेतैर्हयैर्युक्ते महति स्यन्दने स्थितौ।

माधवः पाण्डवश्चैव दिव्यौ शङ्खौ प्रदध्मतुः।।1.14।।
1-14.transliteration:
tataḥ śhvetairhayairyukte mahati syandane sthitau
mādhavaḥ pāṇḍavaśhchaiva divyau śhaṅkhau pradadhmatuḥ

translation.simple: Then, from their magnificent chariot, pulled by radiant white horses, Lord Krishna and Arjuna sounded their divine conch shells. It was a sacred moment of pure resonance.
translation.deep: From a splendid chariot, guided by pure white horses, Lord Krishna, the beloved Madhava, and Arjuna, the devoted Pandava, blew their celestial conch shells. This act wasn't merely a sound of war, but a profound declaration of dharma's unwavering presence, a call from the Divine to uphold righteousness, even in the most challenging of times.
translation.essence: The sacred sound of Krishna and Arjuna's conches, from their radiant chariot, marked a divine beginning, heralding truth and guiding light even as conflict arose.

1-15.sanskrit:
पाञ्चजन्यं हृषीकेशो देवदत्तं धनंजयः।

पौण्ड्रं दध्मौ महाशङ्खं भीमकर्मा वृकोदरः।।1.15।।
1-15.transliteration:
pāñchajanyaṁ hṛiṣhīkeśho devadattaṁ dhanañjayaḥ
pauṇḍraṁ dadhmau mahā-śhaṅkhaṁ bhīma-karmā vṛikodaraḥ

translation.simple: Lord Hrishikesha, Krishna, blew His conch, Pañcajanya. Arjuna, also known as Dhananjaya, sounded his conch, Devadatta. And Bhima, known for his mighty deeds, blew his great conch, Paundra.
translation.deep: The scene unfolds with the divine presence of Lord Krishna, Hrishikesha, the controller of our senses, sounding His auspicious conch, Pañcajanya. Then, Arjuna, Dhananjaya, who had conquered immense wealth, blew his mighty conch, Devadatta. Following them, Bhima, known for his formidable strength and actions, resonated the air with his powerful conch, Paundra. These sacred sounds were not merely battle cries, but a profound call to dharma, setting the stage for the unfolding of divine will.
translation.essence: With Lord Krishna leading, His devoted warriors, Arjuna and Bhima, blew their mighty conches, symbolizing the clarion call of dharma. These powerful sounds heralded a moment of profound spiritual significance, reminding us of the divine orchestration in every moment of our journey.

1-16.sanskrit:
अनन्तविजयं राजा कुन्तीपुत्रो युधिष्ठिरः।

नकुलः सहदेवश्च सुघोषमणिपुष्पकौ।।1.16।।
1-16.transliteration:
anantavijayaṁ rājā kuntī-putro yudhiṣhṭhiraḥ
nakulaḥ sahadevaśhcha sughoṣha-maṇipuṣhpakau

translation.simple: King Yudhishthira, the noble son of Kunti, blew his sacred conch, Anantavijaya. His devoted brothers, Nakula and Sahadeva, also sounded their conches, Sughosha and Manipushpaka, joining the sacred call.
translation.deep: Beyond merely listing names, this verse gently draws our attention to the spiritual readiness of each devoted Pandava. King Yudhishthira's conch, Anantavijaya, whispers of eternal triumph. Nakula's Sughosha, with its sweet sound, and Sahadeva's Manipushpaka, like a blossoming jewel, all contribute to the symphony of dharma. Each sacred sound is a heartfelt prayer, a declaration of righteous intent, and a deep surrender to the divine will before the great battle unfolds.
translation.essence: The Pandava brothers, Yudhishthira, Nakula, and Sahadeva, each sounded their distinctive conches – Anantavijaya, Sughosha, and Manipushpaka. These sacred calls collectively echo their unwavering devotion and firm resolve to uphold dharma as they prepare for destiny's challenge.

1-17.sanskrit:
काश्यश्च परमेष्वासः शिखण्डी च महारथः।

धृष्टद्युम्नो विराटश्च सात्यकिश्चापराजितः।।1.17।।
1-17.transliteration:
kāśhyaśhcha parameṣhvāsaḥ śhikhaṇḍī cha mahā-rathaḥ
dhṛiṣhṭadyumno virāṭaśhcha sātyakiśh chāparājitaḥ

translation.simple: And among them are the great Kaashya, whose bow is mighty, and Shikhandi, a valiant charioteer. There is also Dhrishtadyumna, and King Virata, and the unconquerable Satyaki.
translation.deep: This verse gently reminds us of the many distinguished souls assembled, each a symbol of strength and virtue in their own way. Kaashya, with his mastery; Shikhandi, a great warrior; Dhrishtadyumna, a leader; Virata, a king; and Satyaki, ever victorious. Their presence reflects the diverse powers and unwavering resolve gathered for a righteous cause, much like the inner strengths we invoke for our own spiritual journey.
translation.essence: Let your heart acknowledge the vast array of strengths and unwavering spirits that stand ready, both within and around you, as you face life's noble challenges.

1-18.sanskrit:
द्रुपदो द्रौपदेयाश्च सर्वशः पृथिवीपते।

सौभद्रश्च महाबाहुः शङ्खान्दध्मुः पृथक्पृथक्।।1.18।।
1-18.transliteration:
drupado draupadeyāśhcha sarvaśhaḥ pṛithivī-pate
saubhadraśhcha mahā-bāhuḥ śhaṅkhāndadhmuḥ pṛithak pṛithak

translation.simple: Then, the respected King Drupada, along with Draupadi's brave sons, and the mighty Abhimanyu, son of Subhadra, each sounded their conch shells. Their individual calls filled the air, signifying readiness for the sacred task.
translation.deep: In this moment before the great spiritual teaching begins, we hear the individual sacred calls of Drupada, the brave sons of Draupadi, and the powerful Abhimanyu. Each conch sound is a personal declaration of faith and courage, a dedication to truth from unique hearts. Together, these sounds blend, heralding the profound spiritual journey that is about to unfold.
translation.essence: This verse gently reminds us that even within a grand, collective purpose, each soul offers its unique strength and dedication. The individual sounds of the conches, blown by these great warriors, symbolize the diverse expressions of devotion uniting for a righteous cause.

1-19.sanskrit:
स घोषो धार्तराष्ट्राणां हृदयानि व्यदारयत्।

नभश्च पृथिवीं चैव तुमुलो व्यनुनादयन्।।1.19।।
1-19.transliteration:
sa ghoṣho dhārtarāṣhṭrāṇāṁ hṛidayāni vyadārayat
nabhaśhcha pṛithivīṁ chaiva tumulo nunādayan

translation.simple: The grand sound of the conch shells filled the vast sky and the wide earth. It touched the hearts of the Kaurava warriors deeply, stirring their very core.
translation.deep: This powerful reverberation, spanning heaven and earth, was not merely an earthly sound. It was a divine pronouncement, causing a profound tremor in the hearts of those who stood against the path of dharma. It subtly reminds us that even before any action, the spiritual force of righteousness can evoke deep introspection and a quiet sense of foreboding in those whose hearts are not aligned with truth.
translation.essence: The divine sound, filling all creation, profoundly resonated within the hearts of the opposing side, a powerful whisper of dharma's strength.

1-20.sanskrit:
अथ व्यवस्थितान् दृष्ट्वा धार्तराष्ट्रान्कपिध्वजः।

प्रवृत्ते शस्त्रसंपाते धनुरुद्यम्य पाण्डवः।।1.20।।
1-20.transliteration:
atha vyavasthitān dṛiṣhṭvā dhārtarāṣhṭrān kapi-dhwajaḥ
pravṛitte śhastra-sampāte dhanurudyamya pāṇḍavaḥ
hṛiṣhīkeśhaṁ tadā vākyam idam āha mahī-pate

translation.simple: Then, Arjuna, with Hanuman on his banner, looked upon the sons of Dhritarashtra, ready for battle. As the exchange of weapons commenced, he calmly lifted his bow.
translation.deep: At that pivotal moment, Arjuna, whose flag bore the image of the devoted Hanuman, perceived the formations of his kinsmen. Even as the first clashes of weapons echoed in the air, he deliberately raised his magnificent bow, preparing himself to face the unfolding dharma, yet perhaps with an unspoken yearning for clarity.
translation.essence: Arjuna, with Hanuman on his standard, surveyed the opposing host. As the battle's clang began, he calmly raised his bow, ready to fulfill his role.

1-21.sanskrit:
अर्जुन उवाच

हृषीकेशं तदा वाक्यमिदमाह महीपते।

सेनयोरुभयोर्मध्ये रथं स्थापय मेऽच्युत।।1.21।।
1-21.transliteration:
arjuna uvācha
senayor ubhayor madhye rathaṁ sthāpaya me ’chyuta

translation.simple: Arjuna then spoke to Lord Krishna, who guides all our senses. He humbly requested, "O unfailing Lord, please place my chariot exactly between these two great armies."
translation.deep: With a heart seeking profound understanding as the momentous conflict loomed, Arjuna turned to Lord Krishna, acknowledging Him as Hrishikesha, the inner controller of all senses, and Acyuta, the infallible, never-failing Supreme Being. He earnestly requested, "O Lord, guide my chariot to stand precisely in the midst of both armies. Let me witness this unfolding reality through Your divine arrangement."
translation.essence: Arjuna, turning to the Lord who controls his senses and is eternally unfailing, gently requested Him to position his chariot directly between the two assembled forces, seeking clarity before the momentous event.

1-22.transliteration:
yāvadetān nirīkṣhe ’haṁ yoddhu-kāmān avasthitān
kairmayā saha yoddhavyam asmin raṇa-samudyame

translation.simple: Oh Krishna, let me look upon all those who stand here, eager to wage war. I wish to truly see with whom I must engage in this great undertaking of battle.
translation.deep: Arjuna, with a heart heavy yet resolved, asks to truly behold those arrayed for battle. He wishes to know the faces of those with whom he is destined to engage, seeking a deeper understanding of his duty in this momentous and challenging conflict.
translation.essence: The core of this moment is Arjuna's earnest request to Krishna: to fully behold those standing ready for battle. He wishes to understand his adversaries before dedicating himself to the momentous fight ahead.

1-23.sanskrit:
योत्स्यमानानवेक्षेऽहं य एतेऽत्र समागताः।

धार्तराष्ट्रस्य दुर्बुद्धेर्युद्धे प्रियचिकीर्षवः।।1.23।।
1-23.transliteration:
yotsyamānān avekṣhe ’haṁ ya ete ’tra samāgatāḥ
dhārtarāṣhṭrasya durbuddher yuddhe priya-chikīrṣhavaḥ

translation.simple: My dear Krishna, please let me observe all those who have assembled here, prepared to fight. I wish to see the hearts of those who, out of misguided loyalty, have come to serve the wicked son of Dhritarashtra in this great war.
translation.deep: In this moment, Arjuna seeks to understand the very souls arrayed against him. He yearns to gaze upon those who, despite their kinship, stand with the misguided Duryodhana, desiring to please one who walks a path of unrighteousness. This request reflects his deep contemplation before the daunting task ahead, a quiet search for clarity amidst the impending conflict.
translation.essence: Arjuna desires to clearly see all assembled, especially those aligned with the misguided Duryodhana, as he quietly prepares his heart for the dharma ahead.

1-24.sanskrit:
संजय उवाच

एवमुक्तो हृषीकेशो गुडाकेशेन भारत।

सेनयोरुभयोर्मध्ये स्थापयित्वा रथोत्तमम्।।1.24।।
1-24.transliteration:
sañjaya uvācha
evam ukto hṛiṣhīkeśho guḍākeśhena bhārata
senayor ubhayor madhye sthāpayitvā rathottamam

translation.simple: Sanjaya narrated: When Arjuna expressed his heartfelt desire, Lord Hrishikesha, with serene grace, brought their splendid chariot to a gentle halt, right in the heart of both grand armies.
translation.deep: Sanjaya continued, unveiling a beautiful moment of divine interaction: Upon hearing the request of Arjuna, the 'conqueror of ignorance,' Lord Hrishikesha, the 'master of all senses,' lovingly steered their magnificent chariot to a perfect stop between the two opposing forces. This was not merely a physical act, but the Lord's tender response, creating a sacred pause and placing His dear devotee precisely where the deepest spiritual wisdom was about to be revealed, a beacon of peace amidst the looming conflict.
translation.essence: Responding to Arjuna's sincere plea, Lord Krishna gently positioned the divine chariot amidst the armies, setting the stage for the unfolding of profound spiritual truth.

1-25.sanskrit:
भीष्मद्रोणप्रमुखतः सर्वेषां च महीक्षिताम्।

उवाच पार्थ पश्यैतान्समवेतान्कुरूनिति।।1.25।।
1-25.transliteration:
bhīṣhma-droṇa-pramukhataḥ sarveṣhāṁ cha mahī-kṣhitām
uvācha pārtha paśhyaitān samavetān kurūn iti

translation.simple: In the presence of revered warriors like Bhishma and Drona, and all the assembled kings, Lord Krishna gently spoke to Arjuna, 'My dear Partha, behold these Kuru warriors, all gathered together.'
translation.deep: Lord Krishna, as Arjuna's divine guide and charioteer, directs his gaze to the formidable array of warriors, drawing his attention to his beloved elders, Bhishma and Drona, and all the rulers. This tender instruction to 'behold' is not just about seeing with the eyes, but about preparing Arjuna's heart to fully absorb the gravity of the situation and the spiritual journey that is about to unfold.
translation.essence: With loving compassion, Lord Krishna asks Arjuna to calmly observe all the assembled warriors, including his cherished elders, preparing his mind for the profound spiritual lessons that lie ahead.

1-26.transliteration:
tatrāpaśhyat sthitān pārthaḥ pitṝīn atha pitāmahān
āchāryān mātulān bhrātṝīn putrān pautrān sakhīṁs tathā
śhvaśhurān suhṛidaśh chaiva senayor ubhayor api

translation.simple: As Arjuna stood on the battleground, he looked across and saw his own family and respected elders. He recognized his fathers, grandfathers, revered teachers, beloved uncles, brothers, his sons and grandsons, and even his cherished friends, all arrayed before him.
translation.deep: In that pivotal moment, Arjuna's eyes absorbed the sight of all his dear relations, not merely as an opposing army, but as individuals with whom he shared deep bonds. This profound recognition of elders, mentors, family, and friends standing ready for battle surely brought a quiet introspection to his heart, revealing the immense personal weight of the conflict that lay ahead.
translation.essence: Arjuna's heart filled with a poignant stillness as he recognized his entire network of beloved relations—elders, teachers, family, and friends—standing on the battlefield, bringing the gravity of the moment into sharp, personal focus.

1-27.sanskrit:
श्वशुरान्सुहृदश्चैव सेनयोरुभयोरपि।

तान्समीक्ष्य स कौन्तेयः सर्वान्बन्धूनवस्थितान्।।1.27।।
1-27.transliteration:
tān samīkṣhya sa kaunteyaḥ sarvān bandhūn avasthitān
kṛipayā parayāviṣhṭo viṣhīdann idam abravīt

translation.simple: Arjuna, the son of Kunti, surveyed the scene, beholding his fathers-in-law, cherished friends, and all his relatives present in both armies.
translation.deep: As Arjuna, the son of Kunti, cast his gaze across the assembled warriors, he recognized them not merely as combatants, but as his own fathers-in-law, his cherished friends, and all his beloved kinsmen, standing in both formations. This profound realization touched the deepest parts of his being, revealing the intensely personal nature of the impending struggle.
translation.essence: This moment unveils Arjuna's heart, filled with tender feelings as he recognizes his own beloved family and friends amidst the opposing forces. It highlights the profound inner conflict that arises when our personal affections meet the path of duty.

1-28.sanskrit:
अर्जुन उवाच

कृपया परयाऽऽविष्टो विषीदन्निदमब्रवीत्।

दृष्ट्वेमं स्वजनं कृष्ण युयुत्सुं समुपस्थितम्।।1.28।।
1-28.transliteration:
arjuna uvācha
dṛiṣhṭvemaṁ sva-janaṁ kṛiṣhṇa yuyutsuṁ samupasthitam

translation.simple: Arjuna then spoke, his heart filled with a profound compassion. Seeing his own kin arrayed on the battlefield, ready to fight, he felt a deep sadness, O Krishna.
translation.deep: At this juncture, Arjuna's heart overflows with a profound sense of compassion. The sight of his own dear relatives, arrayed and poised for conflict, fills him with deep sorrow. This moment reveals the tender and complex nature of the human spirit, where personal affection can momentarily overshadow the call of duty. He is moved to speak, burdened by the realization of the impending clash among those he holds dear, turning to Krishna in his distress.
translation.essence: The core message here is the initial awakening of Arjuna's spiritual dilemma: how to reconcile deep compassion for his kin with the immediate call to battle. It beautifully illustrates the human heart's capacity for profound feeling and sets the scene for the divine wisdom that is about to unfold.

1-29.sanskrit:
सीदन्ति मम गात्राणि मुखं च परिशुष्यति।

वेपथुश्च शरीरे मे रोमहर्षश्च जायते।।1.29।।
1-29.transliteration:
sīdanti mama gātrāṇi mukhaṁ cha pariśhuṣhyati
vepathuśh cha śharīre me roma-harṣhaśh cha jāyate

translation.simple: My body feels weary, and my mouth is parched. A shiver runs through me, and my hair stands on end, reflecting the deep turmoil within my soul.
translation.deep: This verse beautifully portrays Arjuna's profound human vulnerability. His physical reactions—weak limbs, dry mouth, trembling, and horripilation—are not mere symptoms but a deep expression of a heart grappling with immense moral conflict and the impending sorrow of war. It signifies a spiritual unrest that naturally precedes a moment of divine revelation and the search for ultimate truth.
translation.essence: In moments of overwhelming inner conflict, our bodies often mirror the deep struggle within. This verse reminds us that such profound disquiet is a natural part of the human journey, often serving as a profound call for surrender and the yearning for divine wisdom.

1-30.sanskrit:
गाण्डीवं स्रंसते हस्तात्त्वक्चैव परिदह्यते।

न च शक्नोम्यवस्थातुं भ्रमतीव च मे मनः।।1.30।।
1-30.transliteration:
gāṇḍīvaṁ sraṁsate hastāt tvak chaiva paridahyate
na cha śhaknomy avasthātuṁ bhramatīva cha me manaḥ

translation.simple: My mighty bow, Gaṇḍīva, feels loose in my hand, and a warmth spreads through my skin. I can hardly stand steady, and my mind feels utterly disoriented, as if spinning.
translation.deep: This intense physical and mental distress reveals Arjuna's profound inner conflict. The slipping bow is not just a loss of grip, but a symbol of his wavering resolve. The burning skin and unsteady posture speak to a soul overwhelmed by sorrow and doubt, while his reeling mind reflects a heart grappling with the immense spiritual and ethical challenge before him, seeking divine wisdom amidst his turmoil.
translation.essence: This verse beautifully captures the universal human experience of profound emotional and mental struggle when faced with life's greatest dilemmas, reminding us that such moments lead us to seek deeper truth and guidance.

1-31.sanskrit:
निमित्तानि च पश्यामि विपरीतानि केशव।

न च श्रेयोऽनुपश्यामि हत्वा स्वजनमाहवे।।1.31।।
1-31.transliteration:
nimittāni cha paśhyāmi viparītāni keśhava
na cha śhreyo ’nupaśhyāmi hatvā sva-janam āhave

translation.simple: O Krishna, I observe only unfavorable signs all around me. I cannot perceive any ultimate good or blessing in killing my own loved ones in this battle.
translation.deep: My dear Keshava, my spirit is troubled, for I witness only inauspicious portents. My heart cannot envision any true welfare or spiritual benefit arising from the act of taking the lives of my own kinsmen in this dreadful conflict. A profound sadness fills me, questioning the very essence of such a victory.
translation.essence: Arjuna, overwhelmed by grief, sees only bad omens and no spiritual merit in a war that demands the lives of his beloved family.

1-32.sanskrit:
न काङ्क्षे विजयं कृष्ण न च राज्यं सुखानि च।

किं नो राज्येन गोविन्द किं भोगैर्जीवितेन वा।।1.32।।
1-32.transliteration:
na kāṅkṣhe vijayaṁ kṛiṣhṇa na cha rājyaṁ sukhāni cha
kiṁ no rājyena govinda kiṁ bhogair jīvitena vā

translation.simple: O Krishna, I do not long for victory, nor do I seek a kingdom or its comforts. What use is a kingdom to me, O Govinda? What good are enjoyments, or even life itself, when faced with such a heavy cost?
translation.deep: Arjuna's heart is heavy, questioning the true worth of worldly gains like victory, power, and pleasure when they come at the cost of immense suffering and the breaking of sacred bonds. This profound moment reflects a spiritual insight: is external triumph truly victory if it compromises inner peace and dharma? He suggests that life's deeper value transcends fleeting material desires.
translation.essence: Overwhelmed by compassion, Arjuna expresses detachment from all worldly triumphs, questioning the value of a kingdom or pleasures gained through sorrow, and yearning for a higher purpose beyond mere acquisition.

1-33.sanskrit:
येषामर्थे काङ्क्षितं नो राज्यं भोगाः सुखानि च।

त इमेऽवस्थिता युद्धे प्राणांस्त्यक्त्वा धनानि च।।1.33।।
1-33.transliteration:
yeṣhām arthe kāṅkṣhitaṁ no rājyaṁ bhogāḥ sukhāni cha
ta ime ’vasthitā yuddhe prāṇāṁs tyaktvā dhanāni cha

translation.simple: These are the very ones for whom we longed for kingdoms, pleasures, and comfort. Yet, here they stand in this war, ready to give up their lives and all their wealth.
translation.deep: My heart is filled with anguish, Lord, seeing those for whom I wished every joy and a glorious kingdom. They now face me on this battlefield, prepared to relinquish their very existence and earthly possessions. This moment profoundly reveals the sorrow woven into worldly desires and the painful paradox of fighting those we hold dear.
translation.essence: The pain of seeing beloved ones, for whom we desire prosperity, now standing as adversaries ready to sacrifice everything, highlights the profound sorrow tied to worldly attachments.

1-34.sanskrit:
आचार्याः पितरः पुत्रास्तथैव च पितामहाः।

मातुलाः श्चशुराः पौत्राः श्यालाः सम्बन्धिनस्तथा।।1.34।।
1-34.transliteration:
āchāryāḥ pitaraḥ putrās tathaiva cha pitāmahāḥ
mātulāḥ śhvaśhurāḥ pautrāḥ śhyālāḥ sambandhinas tathā

translation.simple: Arjuna gazed upon his revered teachers, his fathers, and his sons. He saw his grandfathers, his maternal uncles, and his fathers-in-law. Even his grandsons, brothers-in-law, and many other relatives were present before him.
translation.deep: In this moment, Arjuna's heart was filled with a poignant realization as he identified a vast network of cherished relationships. He recognized those who had taught him, those who had nurtured him, and those who were a part of his future generations. This verse softly speaks of the profound emotional bonds that tie us to family and community, revealing the deep challenge faced when these sacred connections are brought into conflict.
translation.essence: This verse tenderly illuminates the intricate web of human relationships—teachers, family, and kinsmen—reflecting the natural affection and reverence we hold for those who are dear to us, and the inherent difficulty in facing them as adversaries.

1-35.sanskrit:
एतान्न हन्तुमिच्छामि घ्नतोऽपि मधुसूदन।

अपि त्रैलोक्यराज्यस्य हेतोः किं नु महीकृते।।1.35।।
1-35.transliteration:
etān na hantum ichchhāmi ghnato ’pi madhusūdana
api trailokya-rājyasya hetoḥ kiṁ nu mahī-kṛite

translation.simple: My dear Lord Madhusudana, I have no wish to harm these loved ones, even if they should choose to harm me. Not even for the vast domain of the three worlds would I desire to strike them down, much less for just this earthly kingdom.
translation.deep: Lord Madhusudana, Arjuna reveals a heart overflowing with deep compassion and inner turmoil. He states that he cannot bring himself to harm his dear relatives, even if they were to turn against him. This reluctance stems not just from attachment, but a profound revulsion at the thought of gaining any kingdom, even the dominion over three worlds, at such a painful cost. His words reflect a soul yearning for peace over power, rejecting victory stained with the blood of loved ones.
translation.essence: The essence of this verse lies in Arjuna's deep compassion and his unwavering refusal to harm his own kin. He firmly declares to Lord Krishna that even the kingship of all three worlds, let alone this earthly realm, is not worth the sin of fighting his relatives. It highlights his profound emotional and spiritual reluctance to engage in such a battle.

1-36.transliteration:
nihatya dhārtarāṣhṭrān naḥ kā prītiḥ syāj janārdana
pāpam evāśhrayed asmān hatvaitān ātatāyinaḥ

translation.simple: O Lord, what joy could truly be ours if we were to take the lives of these sons of Dhritarashtra? Even though they act as aggressors, we feel that only sin would befall us by killing them.
translation.deep: Arjuna, in his profound dilemma, turns to Lord Krishna, questioning the very nature of happiness that might stem from battle. He feels that even against those who act as enemies, taking the lives of his own kin would only lead to a burden of sin, rather than the pure, lasting joy that comes from righteous action.
translation.essence: Arjuna expresses his anguish, believing that no real happiness could come from killing his relatives, even if they are aggressors, and that such an act would only incur sin.

1-37.sanskrit:
तस्मान्नार्हा वयं हन्तुं धार्तराष्ट्रान्स्वबान्धवान्।

स्वजनं हि कथं हत्वा सुखिनः स्याम माधव।।1.37।।
1-37.transliteration:
tasmān nārhā vayaṁ hantuṁ dhārtarāṣhṭrān sa-bāndhavān 
sva-janaṁ hi kathaṁ hatvā sukhinaḥ syāma mādhava

translation.simple: Arjuna shares his deep reluctance to fight, feeling it is improper to harm his own relatives, the sons of Dhritarashtra. He humbly asks Lord Madhava how true happiness could ever come from such a painful act against one's own kin.
translation.deep: In this verse, Arjuna expresses a profound moral dilemma, questioning the very foundation of happiness when it involves conflict with one's own family. He turns to Lord Madhava, seeking understanding of how any outward victory could lead to inner peace if it necessitates profound sorrow and harm to beloved relatives. It’s a heartfelt reflection on the spiritual weight of our decisions and the true nature of lasting joy.
translation.essence: Arjuna's heart is troubled, questioning how true and lasting happiness can ever arise from harming his own family members. He seeks a path of peace and genuine joy, free from such profound sorrow.

1-38.sanskrit:
यद्यप्येते न पश्यन्ति लोभोपहतचेतसः।

कुलक्षयकृतं दोषं मित्रद्रोहे च पातकम्।।1.38।।
1-38.transliteration:
yady apy ete na paśhyanti lobhopahata-chetasaḥ
kula-kṣhaya-kṛitaṁ doṣhaṁ mitra-drohe cha pātakam

translation.simple: Even though their minds are clouded by greed, they cannot perceive the fault in destroying their own family, nor the sin in turning against their friends.
translation.deep: When the heart is consumed by the fire of greed, dear one, the wisdom to discern right from wrong becomes obscured. These souls, lost in their desires, cannot recognize the profound spiritual harm in shattering their ancestral lineage or the grievous sin in betraying those they should cherish as companions. Their inner vision is clouded, preventing them from understanding the true cost of their actions.
translation.essence: A heart clouded by greed loses its inner light, failing to see the profound truth of sacred family bonds and the sin of turning against loved ones.

1-39.sanskrit:
कथं न ज्ञेयमस्माभिः पापादस्मान्निवर्तितुम्।

कुलक्षयकृतं दोषं प्रपश्यद्भिर्जनार्दन।।1.39।।
1-39.transliteration:
kathaṁ na jñeyam asmābhiḥ pāpād asmān nivartitum
kula-kṣhaya-kṛitaṁ doṣhaṁ prapaśhyadbhir janārdana

translation.simple: O Krishna, when we can clearly see the great wrong in destroying our own family, why should we not know to turn away from such a grave sin?
translation.deep: Arjuna questions O Janardana, why, when we fully perceive the profound moral degradation caused by annihilating our own lineage, should we not possess the wisdom to abstain from this devastating sin? His heart is deeply troubled by the dire consequences, seeking a path of righteousness over one that shatters family bonds and social order.
translation.essence: This verse captures Arjuna's anguish as he grapples with the immense sin of fratricide. He yearns for wisdom to avoid the destruction of his family, questioning why, when the moral error is so evident, one would not choose to withdraw from such a devastating act, seeking peace and dharma instead.

1-40.sanskrit:
कुलक्षये प्रणश्यन्ति कुलधर्माः सनातनाः।

धर्मे नष्टे कुलं कृत्स्नमधर्मोऽभिभवत्युत।।1.40।।
1-40.transliteration:
kula-kṣhaye praṇaśhyanti kula-dharmāḥ sanātanāḥ
dharme naṣhṭe kulaṁ kṛitsnam adharmo ’bhibhavaty uta

translation.simple: When a family line is destroyed, its eternal traditions and sacred duties are lost. And when these righteous ways are forgotten, unrighteousness surely takes hold of the entire family.
translation.deep: This verse gently unveils the profound truth that when the sacred bonds and ancient traditions of a family are shattered, the very light of righteousness within them begins to fade. As this divine light diminishes, unrighteousness starts to cast its shadow over the entire lineage, subtly guiding hearts away from their spiritual path and the harmony of divine principles.
translation.essence: The loss of a family's eternal duties invites unrighteousness to darken its path, moving all away from the light of Dharma.

1-41.sanskrit:
अधर्माभिभवात्कृष्ण प्रदुष्यन्ति कुलस्त्रियः।

स्त्रीषु दुष्टासु वार्ष्णेय जायते वर्णसङ्करः।।1.41।।
1-41.transliteration:
adharmābhibhavāt kṛiṣhṇa praduṣhyanti kula-striyaḥ
strīṣhu duṣhṭāsu vārṣhṇeya jāyate varṇa-saṅkaraḥ

translation.simple: Arjuna expresses his sorrow, O Krishna, that when unrighteousness prevails, the virtuous women of families may lose their purity. He fears that when this happens, O descendant of Vrishni, the natural order of society becomes disturbed.
translation.deep: This verse reflects Arjuna's profound concern for the spiritual and moral fabric of society. He underscores the sacred role of women in maintaining the purity and values of a family, which in turn influences the broader community. The lament is a spiritual insight into how a descent into unrighteousness can first touch the sanctity of the home, leading to a disturbance in the divine order and harmony of human relations.
translation.essence: Purity within families, upheld by virtuous women, is vital for a harmonious society. When unrighteousness flourishes, this sacred purity is threatened, leading to confusion in the social order.

1-42.sanskrit:
सङ्करो नरकायैव कुलघ्नानां कुलस्य च।

पतन्ति पितरो ह्येषां लुप्तपिण्डोदकक्रियाः।।1.42।।
1-42.transliteration:
saṅkaro narakāyaiva kula-ghnānāṁ kulasya cha
patanti pitaro hy eṣhāṁ lupta-piṇḍodaka-kriyāḥ

translation.simple: Arjuna grieves, thinking that when family traditions fade, it brings sadness to all. He feels that even our ancestors, who depend on loving offerings, might suffer if these sacred rituals are lost.
translation.deep: This verse reflects Arjuna’s deep concern that the collapse of righteous family structures leads to spiritual disarray for living generations. He fears it also affects our beloved ancestors, as the traditional rites of remembrance and sustenance, meant to honor them, would cease. It highlights the profound spiritual bond within a family across time and the ripple effects of upholding or neglecting one's sacred duties.
translation.essence: It reminds us that our family's spiritual well-being, across generations, is deeply intertwined with preserving sacred traditions and performing our duties with love and respect.

1-43.sanskrit:
दोषैरेतैः कुलघ्नानां वर्णसङ्करकारकैः।

उत्साद्यन्ते जातिधर्माः कुलधर्माश्च शाश्वताः।।1.43।।
1-43.transliteration:
doṣhair etaiḥ kula-ghnānāṁ varṇa-saṅkara-kārakaiḥ
utsādyante jāti-dharmāḥ kula-dharmāśh cha śhāśhvatāḥ

translation.simple: Actions that tear families apart and cause confusion in our shared ways of life quietly uproot the eternal duties meant for both family and community.
translation.deep: These grave faults, arising from actions that dismantle family harmony and cause confusion in the sacred order of our lives, lead to the silent erosion of the everlasting duties meant for our families and communities. When these ancient spiritual pillars are weakened, the very fabric of harmony and well-being, passed down through generations, begins to unravel, affecting not just one soul, but the collective spirit.
translation.essence: The disruption of family and ancient traditions quietly unravels the eternal duties that sustain our spiritual and social harmony. It gently reminds us of the preciousness of preserving our sacred heritage.

1-44.sanskrit:
उत्सन्नकुलधर्माणां मनुष्याणां जनार्दन।

नरकेऽनियतं वासो भवतीत्यनुशुश्रुम।।1.44।।
1-44.transliteration:
utsanna-kula-dharmāṇāṁ manuṣhyāṇāṁ janārdana
narake ‘niyataṁ vāso bhavatītyanuśhuśhruma

translation.simple: O Krishna, we have heard from the wise that when a family's sacred traditions are lost, its members may dwell in a state of suffering for a long, unfixed time.
translation.deep: Arjuna, in his heartfelt concern, expresses a profound truth about 'kuladharma' – the sacred moral and ethical fabric of a family. He understands that these traditions are not mere customs but vital anchors for spiritual well-being and societal harmony. When these precious values are neglected or destroyed, he fears that a lasting state of sorrow, a kind of 'naraka' or spiritual distress, awaits. This isn't just a physical place, but a condition of being where peace and joy are elusive. His words serve as a gentle reminder to cherish and uphold the righteous heritage passed down through generations.
translation.essence: This verse highlights Arjuna's deep worry: the loss of a family's righteous traditions can lead to prolonged suffering and a troubled existence, emphasizing the importance of preserving our spiritual heritage.

1-45.sanskrit:
अहो बत महत्पापं कर्तुं व्यवसिता वयम्।

यद्राज्यसुखलोभेन हन्तुं स्वजनमुद्यताः।।1.45।।
1-45.transliteration:
aho bata mahat pāpaṁ kartuṁ vyavasitā vayam
yad rājya-sukha-lobhena hantuṁ sva-janam udyatāḥ

translation.simple: Alas, what a grave wrong we are poised to do. Enticed by the allure of a kingdom and its fleeting joys, we are prepared to take the lives of our very own people.
translation.deep: Here, a deep sorrow wells up, recognizing a terrible error about to unfold. It's the moment when one realizes that the pursuit of earthly comforts and power, like a kingdom's transient glory, can lead us to overlook our most sacred bonds. The heart aches at the thought of acting against one's own, driven by desires that are ultimately fleeting. This realization is a quiet turning point, hinting at the deeper wisdom that true happiness lies beyond such temporary gains and the grave actions they can inspire.
translation.essence: The sorrowful insight that worldly ambitions can blind us to our sacred ties, prompting actions against our very own.

1-46.sanskrit:
यदि मामप्रतीकारमशस्त्रं शस्त्रपाणयः।

धार्तराष्ट्रा रणे हन्युस्तन्मे क्षेमतरं भवेत्।।1.46।।
1-46.transliteration:
yadi mām apratīkāram aśhastraṁ śhastra-pāṇayaḥ
dhārtarāṣhṭrā raṇe hanyus tan me kṣhemataraṁ bhavet

translation.simple: Arjuna, with a heavy heart, feels that if the armed sons of Dhritarashtra were to take his life on the battlefield while he stands unarmed and unresisting, he would find such an end far more peaceful and auspicious for his soul.
translation.deep: This verse gently unveils Arjuna's profound inner turmoil and his boundless compassion. He expresses a poignant desire for a path of non-resistance, contemplating that to be killed by his kinsmen while unarmed would bestow upon him a greater sense of peace and a more sacred outcome than engaging in the fratricidal war. It highlights his spiritual yearning to avoid violence and preserve purity of heart, even at the cost of his own life.
translation.essence: The core feeling here is Arjuna's profound weariness with conflict, making him wish for a peaceful demise at the hands of his kin, rather than engaging in a fight that tears his spirit.

1-47.sanskrit:
सञ्जय उवाच

एवमुक्त्वाऽर्जुनः संख्ये रथोपस्थ उपाविशत्।

विसृज्य सशरं चापं शोकसंविग्नमानसः।।1.47।।
1-47.transliteration:
sañjaya uvācha
evam uktvārjunaḥ saṅkhye rathopastha upāviśhat
visṛijya sa-śharaṁ chāpaṁ śhoka-saṁvigna-mānasaḥ

translation.simple: Sanjaya narrated: After expressing his thoughts, Arjuna quietly sat down on his chariot. He laid aside his bow and arrows, his heart heavy with sorrow.
translation.deep: In this poignant moment, we witness the great warrior Arjuna, not overcome by an enemy, but by profound inner grief. He sets aside his weapons, the very tools of his duty, symbolizing a spirit overwhelmed by sorrow and confusion. This deep pause, born of a heart in anguish, perfectly sets the stage for the divine wisdom that is about to illuminate his path.
translation.essence: Overwhelmed by deep sorrow, Arjuna lays down his weapons and sits, his heart heavy. This act of letting go, born of inner turmoil, makes him receptive to the profound spiritual guidance he is about to receive.

2-1.sanskrit:
सञ्जय उवाच

तं तथा कृपयाऽविष्टमश्रुपूर्णाकुलेक्षणम्।

विषीदन्तमिदं वाक्यमुवाच मधुसूदनः।।2.1।।
2-1.transliteration:
sañjaya uvācha
taṁ tathā kṛipayāviṣhṭamaśhru pūrṇākulekṣhaṇam
viṣhīdantamidaṁ vākyam uvācha madhusūdanaḥ

translation.simple: Sanjaya reported: Seeing Arjuna deeply overcome with compassion, his eyes overflowing with tears and his heart heavy with sorrow, Lord Krishna, the remover of all obstacles (Madhusudana), then spoke these words.
translation.deep: Sanjaya reveals the scene: Arjuna, utterly submerged in a sea of pity, his vision blurred by ceaseless tears, sat despondent on the battlefield. It was precisely at this moment of profound emotional turmoil that Sri Krishna, the slayer of the demon Madhu, began to unfold the eternal wisdom, marking the very beginning of the Bhagavad Gita's divine teachings.
translation.essence: Sanjaya describes Arjuna's intense sorrow and tear-filled distress. At this crucial juncture, Lord Krishna, Madhusudana, steps in to offer His divine and enlightening counsel.

2-2.sanskrit:
श्री भगवानुवाच

कुतस्त्वा कश्मलमिदं विषमे समुपस्थितम्।

अनार्यजुष्टमस्वर्ग्यमकीर्तिकरमर्जुन।।2.2।।
2-2.transliteration:
śhrī bhagavān uvācha
kutastvā kaśhmalamidaṁ viṣhame samupasthitam
anārya-juṣhṭamaswargyam akīrti-karam arjuna

translation.simple: Lord Krishna lovingly asked, 'My dear Arjuna, how has this moment of weakness found its way to you in such a critical time? This feeling is not what noble hearts cherish; it does not uplift, nor does it bring honor.'
translation.deep: Lord Krishna, with His divine wisdom, gently questions Arjuna's sudden despair. He reminds us that moments of doubt and weakness, which do not uplift our spirit or serve our higher purpose, are not fitting for a soul aspiring to divinity. This gentle inquiry encourages us to introspect, to understand the source of our inner turmoil, and to steadfastly turn away from thoughts that dim our inner light and distract us from our path of dharma. It's a call to reclaim our inherent strength and noble spirit.
translation.essence: Lord Krishna, with profound love, asks Arjuna to shake off this moment of weakness. He reminds us that our true nature is noble and strong, and we should always choose thoughts and actions that uplift us spiritually and bring true honor, rather than yielding to despair.

2-3.sanskrit:
क्लैब्यं मा स्म गमः पार्थ नैतत्त्वय्युपपद्यते।

क्षुद्रं हृदयदौर्बल्यं त्यक्त्वोत्तिष्ठ परन्तप।।2.3।।
2-3.transliteration:
klaibyaṁ mā sma gamaḥ pārtha naitat tvayyupapadyate
kṣhudraṁ hṛidaya-daurbalyaṁ tyaktvottiṣhṭha parantapa

translation.simple: Oh Arjuna, do not give in to weakness. Such a lack of resolve does not suit your noble spirit. Cast aside this small faint-heartedness and stand tall, O one who can overcome all obstacles.
translation.deep: Lord Krishna lovingly admonishes Arjuna not to fall into helplessness. He reminds Arjuna that such a lack of inner strength is unfitting for his true spiritual essence. It is a call to awaken from the slumber of despair, to transcend the smallness of a faltering heart, and to stand firm in one's righteous duty, embracing the divine courage that resides within.
translation.essence: This verse is a divine encouragement to overcome all forms of inner weakness. It teaches us to shed our hesitations, rise above small-mindedness, and step forward with courage, embracing our inherent strength to fulfill our life's purpose.

2-4.sanskrit:
अर्जुन उवाच

कथं भीष्ममहं संख्ये द्रोणं च मधुसूदन।

इषुभिः प्रतियोत्स्यामि पूजार्हावरिसूदन।।2.4।।
2-4.transliteration:
arjuna uvācha
kathaṁ bhīṣhmam ahaṁ sankhye droṇaṁ cha madhusūdana
iṣhubhiḥ pratiyotsyāmi pūjārhāvari-sūdana

translation.simple: Arjuna said: O Krishna, how can I possibly fight against revered elders like Bhishma and Drona with my arrows in this battle? They are truly worthy of my worship.
translation.deep: Arjuna spoke, his voice filled with anguish: O Madhusūdana, how can my heart allow me to strike with arrows against Bhishma and Drona in this war? O Slayer of enemies, these are souls who truly deserve my deepest reverence and devotion, not my hostility.
translation.essence: Arjuna's inner conflict surfaces as he questions Krishna, wondering how he can raise his weapons against his beloved teachers and elders, Bhishma and Drona, who are truly worthy of his worship.

2-5.sanskrit:
गुरूनहत्वा हि महानुभावान्

श्रेयो भोक्तुं भैक्ष्यमपीह लोके।

हत्वार्थकामांस्तु गुरूनिहैव

भुञ्जीय भोगान् रुधिरप्रदिग्धान्।।2.5।।
2-5.transliteration:
gurūnahatvā hi mahānubhāvān
śhreyo bhoktuṁ bhaikṣhyamapīha loke
hatvārtha-kāmāṁstu gurūnihaiva
bhuñjīya bhogān rudhira-pradigdhān

translation.simple: Arjuna feels it would be better to live a life of humble simplicity, even sustained by alms, than to take the lives of these noble and respected teachers. For him, any enjoyment gained after such a battle would be forever stained with their very blood.
translation.deep: Arjuna faces an agonizing moral dilemma, preferring a life of renunciation and dependence on charity over the material comforts of a kingdom achieved by slaying his venerable preceptors. He recognizes that even if these teachers are driven by worldly desires, the act of harming them would indelibly stain any future joy, making all achievements born from such violence repugnant to his conscience.
translation.essence: Arjuna profoundly struggles with the thought of enjoying worldly prosperity if it means shedding the blood of his revered teachers, affirming that a humble, righteous life is superior to gains acquired through such grave violence.

2-6.sanskrit:
न चैतद्विद्मः कतरन्नो गरीयो

यद्वा जयेम यदि वा नो जयेयुः।

यानेव हत्वा न जिजीविषाम

स्तेऽवस्थिताः प्रमुखे धार्तराष्ट्राः।।2.6।।
2-6.transliteration:
na chaitadvidmaḥ kataranno garīyo
yadvā jayema yadi vā no jayeyuḥ
yāneva hatvā na jijīviṣhāmas
te ’vasthitāḥ pramukhe dhārtarāṣhṭrāḥ

translation.simple: We truly do not know which path is better for us – whether we should win this battle, or if it would be better for them to conquer us. For truly, we would not wish to live after having slain these very sons of Dhritarashtra, who stand before us on the battlefield.
translation.deep: Here, Arjuna reveals his deep inner turmoil and confusion, admitting he cannot see which outcome—victory or defeat—would truly serve a greater purpose or bring peace. His heart is heavy with compassion, as he expresses a profound unwillingness to continue living should he be forced to kill his own kinsmen, the sons of Dhritarashtra, who stand arrayed against him. This sentiment reflects a soul grappling with immense moral burden, where the potential cost of triumph feels unbearable.
translation.essence: Arjuna confesses his complete inability to know what is truly beneficial, whether to achieve victory or suffer defeat. He states with a heavy heart that he would not desire to live after vanquishing his own relatives, the sons of Dhritarashtra, who are now his opponents. It highlights his moral dilemma and deep sorrow.

2-7.sanskrit:
कार्पण्यदोषोपहतस्वभावः

पृच्छामि त्वां धर्मसंमूढचेताः।

यच्छ्रेयः स्यान्निश्िचतं ब्रूहि तन्मे

शिष्यस्तेऽहं शाधि मां त्वां प्रपन्नम्।।2.7।।
2-7.transliteration:
kārpaṇya-doṣhopahata-svabhāvaḥ
pṛichchhāmi tvāṁ dharma-sammūḍha-chetāḥ
yach-chhreyaḥ syānniśhchitaṁ brūhi tanme
śhiṣhyaste ’haṁ śhādhi māṁ tvāṁ prapannam

translation.simple: My heart feels weak, and my mind is confused about what is right. I humbly ask You, Lord, to clearly tell me what is truly good for me. I am Your surrendered student; please guide me.
translation.deep: A profound weakness and indecision have clouded my natural understanding, leaving my consciousness bewildered about my true purpose and righteous path. With a heart full of trust, I turn to You, my Lord, to reveal that which is ultimately and certainly beneficial. I declare myself Your devoted disciple, having taken complete refuge in Your divine presence. Please, Krishna, illuminate my way and impart Your sacred wisdom.
translation.essence: Overwhelmed by inner weakness and confusion about my duty, I surrender to You as Your disciple. Please instruct me on what is truly best.

2-8.sanskrit:
न हि प्रपश्यामि ममापनुद्या

द्यच्छोकमुच्छोषणमिन्द्रियाणाम्।

अवाप्य भूमावसपत्नमृद्धम्

राज्यं सुराणामपि चाधिपत्यम्।।2.8।।
2-8.transliteration:
na hi prapaśhyāmi mamāpanudyād
yach-chhokam uchchhoṣhaṇam-indriyāṇām
avāpya bhūmāv-asapatnamṛiddhaṁ
rājyaṁ surāṇāmapi chādhipatyam

translation.simple: I simply cannot see how anything in this world could remove this profound sorrow that is drying up my very senses. Not even gaining a prosperous, unrivaled kingdom on earth, or even sovereignty over the celestial beings, would bring an end to this deep pain within me.
translation.deep: My heart feels such an immense grief, O Krishna, that it seems to shrivel my inner being. I am certain that no worldly triumph—not an undisputed reign over all the earth, nor even dominion over the heavens—could possibly quell this deep spiritual agony. It is clear that true peace must come from a source far beyond these temporary achievements.
translation.essence: No amount of earthly power or celestial rule can alleviate the profound sorrow that stirs the soul. Real peace and solace must be found beyond all material achievements and fleeting glories.

2-9.sanskrit:
सञ्जय उवाच

एवमुक्त्वा हृषीकेशं गुडाकेशः परन्तप।

न योत्स्य इति गोविन्दमुक्त्वा तूष्णीं बभूव ह।।2.9।।
2-9.transliteration:
sañjaya uvācha
evam-uktvā hṛiṣhīkeśhaṁ guḍākeśhaḥ parantapa
na yotsya iti govindam uktvā tūṣhṇīṁ babhūva ha

translation.simple: Sanjaya recounted that Arjuna, having poured out his heart to Lord Krishna, the master of all senses, finally declared, "I will not fight." After uttering these words to the Lord, who nourishes and protects all beings, Arjuna fell completely silent.
translation.deep: This moment reveals Arjuna, the mighty warrior and conqueror of inner turmoil, reaching a state of profound stillness. After clearly stating his deep anguish and resolute decision not to engage in battle to Lord Krishna, the very director of his senses, he became utterly silent. This silence was not merely an absence of words, but perhaps a quiet surrender, creating a sacred space within him for the divine wisdom of Govinda to begin its flow. It marks the calm before a profound spiritual awakening.
translation.essence: Having firmly expressed his refusal to fight, Arjuna surrendered into complete silence before the Lord, thereby preparing his heart to receive the profound divine teachings. His quietude was a profound moment of readiness for spiritual instruction.

2-10.sanskrit:
तमुवाच हृषीकेशः प्रहसन्निव भारत।

सेनयोरुभयोर्मध्ये विषीदन्तमिदं वचः।।2.10।।
2-10.transliteration:
tam-uvācha hṛiṣhīkeśhaḥ prahasanniva bhārata
senayorubhayor-madhye viṣhīdantam-idaṁ vachaḥ

translation.simple: In the heart of the battlefield, between the two great armies, Lord Hrishikesha, with a soft, knowing smile, began to speak to Arjuna, who was lost in his distress.
translation.deep: Amidst the hushed tension between the two vast armies, Lord Hrishikesha, the master of all senses, offered Arjuna a gentle, knowing smile. It was a smile of divine compassion, reassuring the despondent warrior that wisdom was about to descend, bringing solace to his troubled heart.
translation.essence: The Lord, with a loving, subtle smile, began to pour forth divine wisdom to Arjuna, who was immersed in grief between the vast armies. It was the moment divine guidance unfolded.

2-11.sanskrit:
श्री भगवानुवाच

अशोच्यानन्वशोचस्त्वं प्रज्ञावादांश्च भाषसे।

गतासूनगतासूंश्च नानुशोचन्ति पण्डिताः।।2.11।।
2-11.transliteration:
śhrī bhagavān uvācha
aśhochyān-anvaśhochas-tvaṁ prajñā-vādānśh cha bhāṣhase
gatāsūn-agatāsūnśh-cha nānuśhochanti paṇḍitāḥ

translation.simple: The Blessed Lord gently revealed: You speak as if you know wisdom, dear one, yet you sorrow for what should not cause grief. Truly wise souls, knowing the true nature of existence, find no reason to lament for either the living or those who have passed on.
translation.deep: The Lord, full of compassion, spoke: You articulate profound thoughts, Arjuna, yet your heart is troubled by sorrow for things that are transient. The truly discerning, those who have glimpsed the eternal truth of the soul, understand that the body is but a temporary garment. Therefore, they remain undisturbed, knowing that the spirit within is never born and never dies. Their peace stems from this unwavering knowledge, transcending the dualities of life and death.
translation.essence: With divine wisdom, the Lord reminds us: True peace comes from understanding the soul's eternal nature, liberating us from grief over the body's temporary journey.

2-12.sanskrit:
न त्वेवाहं जातु नासं न त्वं नेमे जनाधिपाः।

न चैव न भविष्यामः सर्वे वयमतः परम्।।2.12।।
2-12.transliteration:
na tvevāhaṁ jātu nāsaṁ na tvaṁ neme janādhipāḥ
na chaiva na bhaviṣhyāmaḥ sarve vayamataḥ param

translation.simple: Never was there a time when I, Lord Krishna, did not exist, nor you, Arjuna, nor any of these revered leaders. And certainly, none of us will ever cease to be. We all continue our journey eternally.
translation.deep: Lord Krishna lovingly reassures Arjuna of a profound spiritual truth: the eternal nature of the soul. He explains that just as He, the Supreme Being, has always existed and will always exist, so too do all individual souls. What we perceive as birth and death are merely changes in our physical forms or experiences, while our true self, the spirit, remains ever-present, untouched by time's passage.
translation.essence: This verse reminds us that our true spiritual self, the soul, is eternal. We are timeless beings who have always existed and will continue to exist, beyond the temporary changes of the body and the world.

2-13.sanskrit:
देहिनोऽस्मिन्यथा देहे कौमारं यौवनं जरा।

तथा देहान्तरप्राप्तिर्धीरस्तत्र न मुह्यति।।2.13।।
2-13.transliteration:
dehino ’smin yathā dehe kaumāraṁ yauvanaṁ jarā
tathā dehāntara-prāptir dhīras tatra na muhyati

translation.simple: Just as our soul experiences the body's journey through childhood, youth, and old age, so too does it lovingly transition to a new form. A calm and steady heart finds no confusion in this natural process.
translation.deep: Within this fleeting form, the eternal soul patiently observes the body's gentle transformations—from the innocence of childhood, through the vigor of youth, to the wisdom of old age. These are mere coverings that change with time. With the same natural grace, the soul continues its sacred journey, moving from one physical dwelling to another. One whose mind is rooted in spiritual wisdom is never bewildered by these inevitable shifts, understanding the soul's unchanging and everlasting presence.
translation.essence: The soul gently traverses life's stages within the body, and likewise, moves on to a new one. A wise and peaceful heart remains undisturbed by these natural transitions.

2-14.transliteration:
mātrā-sparśhās tu kaunteya śhītoṣhṇa-sukha-duḥkha-dāḥ
āgamāpāyino ’nityās tans-titikṣhasva bhārata

translation.simple: O Arjuna, the encounters our senses have with the world bring feelings of cold and warmth, joy and sorrow. These feelings come and go, they are never permanent. Therefore, dear one, simply learn to bear them with patience.
translation.deep: Beloved seeker, know that the experiences of life—the comfort of warmth, the challenge of cold, the embrace of happiness, and the touch of sorrow—are all fleeting by nature. They arise and then gently fade, much like clouds in the sky. When we truly understand their impermanence, we gain the spiritual strength to not be swayed by them. Cultivating this patient endurance allows our inner spirit to remain tranquil, untroubled by the world's constant flow, and ever connected to a deeper, unchanging peace.
translation.essence: Life's experiences, both pleasant and painful, are temporary. With a steady heart, learn to patiently endure them, finding peace amidst their coming and going.

2-15.sanskrit:
यं हि न व्यथयन्त्येते पुरुषं पुरुषर्षभ।

समदुःखसुखं धीरं सोऽमृतत्वाय कल्पते।।2.15।।
2-15.transliteration:
yaṁ hi na vyathayantyete puruṣhaṁ puruṣharṣhabha
sama-duḥkha-sukhaṁ dhīraṁ so ’mṛitatvāya kalpate

translation.simple: O best of men, the soul that remains undisturbed by the coming and going of joy and sorrow, seeing them with a calm and equal mind, such a steady one is truly fit for eternal peace.
translation.deep: This verse whispers a deep truth: the one who learns not to be swayed by life's fleeting dualities, who meets both joy and sorrow with inner stability, truly begins to walk the path of immortality. This profound steadiness, rooted in wisdom, helps us transcend the changing world and realize the eternal nature of the self.
translation.essence: A soul unperturbed by life's dualities, holding joy and sorrow equally, is destined for lasting liberation.

2-16.sanskrit:
नासतो विद्यते भावो नाभावो विद्यते सतः।

उभयोरपि दृष्टोऽन्तस्त्वनयोस्तत्त्वदर्शिभिः।।2.16।।
2-16.transliteration:
nāsato vidyate bhāvo nābhāvo vidyate sataḥ
ubhayorapi dṛiṣhṭo ’nta stvanayos tattva-darśhibhiḥ
